lessons.title: What farm animals need every day
lessons.html:
What farm animals need every day

Cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and chickens all depend on people to care for them. Good care keeps animals healthy and productive, and it is the law. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes it a crime to be cruel to animals or to neglect them, for example by not giving them food and water.

The five basic needs

  1. Food: enough of the right feed, every day.
  2. Clean water: always available. Animals drink more in hot weather and when they produce milk.
  3. Shelter and comfort: shade in summer, protection from wind and cold, and a clean, dry place to lie down.
  4. Health: prevent disease and treat sick or injured animals quickly.
  5. Freedom from fear and stress: calm handling, enough space and the company of other animals.

Daily care checklist

  • Count the animals in each camp, pen or house. Report any that are missing.
  • Check that water troughs are full and clean, and that floats and pipes work.
  • Give feed at the right time and in the right amount. Check that feed is not mouldy.
  • Clean pens, stalls and houses; remove dung and wet bedding.
  • Check fences and gates.
  • Look at every animal for signs of illness or injury.

Housing for different animals

AnimalHousing needs
CattleCamps with shade, water and good fences; a kraal or crush for handling
Sheep and goatsShelter from cold rain and wind, especially after shearing and at lambing
PigsDry, clean pens with shade; pigs cannot sweat and suffer in heat
ChickensClean house with fresh air, the right temperature, clean litter, feeders and drinkers

lessons.title: Recognising sick animals
lessons.html:
Recognising sick animals

Sick animals often hide their illness. You must learn what a healthy animal looks like so you notice quickly when something is wrong. The earlier a problem is found, the easier it is to treat.

Signs of a healthy animal

  • Bright, clear eyes and alert ears.
  • Eats and drinks normally; ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats) chew the cud when resting.
  • Moves easily and stays with the group.
  • Smooth, shiny coat or clean feathers.
  • Normal dung, not too runny or too hard.
  • Breathes calmly.

Signs of a sick animal

  • Stands alone, head down, or lies down and does not get up.
  • Does not eat or drink; stops chewing the cud.
  • Dull eyes, runny eyes or nose, coughing.
  • Diarrhoea, blood in dung or urine.
  • Limping, swollen joints or wounds.
  • Fast or difficult breathing.
  • Swollen belly (bloat) on the left side in cattle or sheep. This is an emergency.
  • Pale inside of the eyelid in sheep and goats, which can be a sign of worms such as wireworm.
  • Ticks, lice or mange on the skin.

What to do

  1. Do not ignore it. Separate the animal if your supervisor says so, gently and calmly.
  2. Report it to your supervisor immediately: which animal (tag number), where it is and what you saw.
  3. Give treatment only if you have been trained and told to, using the product and dose on the label or from the vet.
  4. Write it in the animal health register.

Notifiable diseases

Some diseases, such as foot-and-mouth disease, are controlled under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 and must be reported to the state veterinarian. Signs such as blisters on the mouth and feet, drooling and sudden lameness in many animals must be reported straight away. Do not move animals until you are told to.

lessons.title: Preventing disease and working safely
lessons.html:
Preventing disease and working safely

Preventing disease

  • Vaccination: the farm follows a vaccination programme planned with the vet. Vaccines must be kept cold in the fridge (not frozen) and used as the label says.
  • Parasite control: dipping or pour-ons for ticks, and dosing for worms, at the times set by the programme.
  • Clean water and feed and clean housing.
  • Biosecurity: keep new or sick animals apart (quarantine) before they join the herd; clean boots and vehicles; keep visitors out of animal houses.
  • Remove dead animals quickly and dispose of them as the farm instructs.

Medicines

Many animal medicines have a withdrawal period: the time after treatment before milk, eggs or meat from that animal may be used. Follow the product label or your vet. Record every treatment: date, animal, product, dose and who gave it.

Working safely with animals

  • Approach calmly from the side where the animal can see you. Talk quietly.
  • Never stand directly behind a cow or horse; they can kick.
  • Be very careful with bulls, rams, boars and mothers with young. Never work alone with a bull.
  • Use a crush or a pen to hold animals for treatment.
  • Wear boots, overalls and gloves. Wash your hands after handling animals, dung or medicines.
  • Some diseases, such as brucellosis and anthrax, can pass from animals to people. Never open the carcass of an animal that died suddenly; report it.
  • Needles are sharp; never recap a used needle and put it in the sharps container.

Key points

  • Animals need food, clean water, shelter, health care and calm handling every day.
  • The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes cruelty and neglect a crime.
  • Know the signs of a healthy and a sick animal; report problems immediately.
  • Prevent disease with vaccination, parasite control, hygiene and quarantine.
  • Follow labels and the vet for doses and withdrawal periods, and record every treatment.
  • Work safely: approach calmly, avoid kicks and never open a carcass of a sudden death.
